report:
## Conclusion: The claim is actually supported by evidence — your skepticism is understandable, but the data lean the other way.

**Key evidence:**

1. **PREDIMED randomized trial** (~7,400 high-risk Spaniards): A Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil reduced major cardiovascular events vs. a low-fat control diet; stroke was the component most clearly reduced (~30% relative risk reduction). The trial was retracted in 2018 over randomization errors at some sites, but the corrected reanalysis found essentially the same results.
   - https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29897866/
   - https://www.bmj.com/content/364/bmj.l341?int_source=trendmd&int_medium=cpc&int_campaign=usage-042019

2. **Three-City Study** (France, 7,625 adults 65+, ~5 years follow-up): "Intensive" olive oil users had a 41% lower stroke incidence than non-users, with plasma oleic acid (a biomarker) supporting the association.
   - https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0b013e318220abeb

3. **Meta-analysis** (Martínez-González et al., *British Journal of Nutrition* 2014; 9 studies, >100,000 participants): Higher olive oil intake was associated with significantly lower risk of stroke and CHD.
   - https://www.myolivea.com/blogs/research/olive-oil-stroke-cardiovascular-meta-analysis-2014

**Important caveats:** Most evidence is observational, so confounding is possible (olive oil users tend to have healthier lifestyles overall). PREDIMED tested a whole Mediterranean dietary pattern, not olive oil in isolation, and benefits likely come partly from *replacing* butter/margarine rather than adding oil on top of an unchanged diet. Still, the consistency across cohorts, biomarkers, meta-analysis, and a randomized trial means the claim is reasonably well-supported — not false.
